The bystander effect is an unfortunate phenomenon of human psychology: People are less likely to help someone in distress when there are more people around. And when someone does help, it takes longer than if they were alone. This is because:

  • You're not sure the victim is in danger, because nobody else is helping.
  • You don't want to go against the herd -- if nobody is helping, you default to following their lead.
  • You don't feel responsible -- the more people around, the less individual responsibility you have for the victim.

To break this effect when you're in a crowd, you can do two things:

  1. Start helping. It's better to annoy someone who is OK than ignore someone who isn't. And this spurs the rest of the crowd to help.
  2. Point to specific people and say something like "you, in the red shirt, call 911". Singling them out as an individual changes their behavior.

Similarly, if you find yourself in danger but nobody steps up, ask one person for help and more will follow.
LPT: Beware the bystander effect. If someone might be in danger but everyone else is unsure, try to give aid anyway. If you need help, single out somebody and ask them.
